An incident response checklist for possible CVE-2026-113867 account abuse


An investigation into CVE-2026-113867 should begin with a version and configuration question, then move to account history only when the relevant XMPP path was present. The flaw could inject outbound stanzas through Thunderbird, but the reviewed sources do not show a universal compromise marker. A disciplined timeline can separate vulnerable systems from confirmed abuse.
Mozilla documented CVE-2026-113867 in MFSA 2026-114 and MFSA 2026-115. Thunderbird did not escape attribute values when serializing outgoing XMPP stanzas. Incoming request values echoed through automatic replies could inject arbitrary stanzas into the authenticated connection.
The flaw was fixed in Thunderbird 158.0.1 and 153.5.1. Mozilla assigns h…
articles.title: An incident response checklist for possible CVE-2026-113867 account abuse

articles.description:
The short version, for everyone: Kengele is a free, open-source alarm for activists. If an activist stops checking in, their trusted contacts are alerted. The hard part is that governments switch the internet off at exactly the moments abductions happen, and during a shutdown everyone goes quiet. This post walks through the Go code that tells "the activist went silent" apart from "the network went silent", with a scenario you can run on your own machine.
Kengele (Swahili for "bell") is an alarm for activists in East Africa. Ukinyamaza, kengele inalia: "if you go quiet, the bell rings." An activist sets a watch window before a protest, a court date or a border crossing ("2pm to 10pm, check in every 90 minutes"). Their check-ins go to three to five guardians. If a check-in does not arrive, e…
articles.title: A dead man's switch that survives an internet shutdown: inside Kengele's deadline engine in Go

articles.description:
Why Secrets Management Is the First Thing You’ll Hit When Switching Clouds


When you move an application from Amazon Web Services to Microsoft Azure, the first thing that usually breaks isn’t the compute layer—it’s the way you keep passwords, API keys, and certificates safe. In AWS many teams rely on AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (or the older AWS Secrets Manager) to fetch values at runtime. Azure’s counterpart is Azure Key Vault.  
Both services provide encryption‑at‑rest, fine‑grained IAM, and versioning, but their SDKs, authentication flows, and naming conventions differ enough that a naïve copy‑paste will throw a ResourceNotFound or an authentication error. This post walks through a concrete, minimal example: reading a secret string from the store in a Node.js Lambda‑style funct…
articles.title: Migrating Secrets Management: AWS Parameter Store vs Azure Key Vault

articles.author: Ved Gupta
articles.description:
Most SQL tutorials stop at syntax (JOIN, GROUP BY, window functions) and leave you guessing when a real production query suddenly slows down.
Understanding why a query is slow means understanding how the database engine actually parses, plans, indexes, and executes it. Passive reading about B-Trees, query plans, and transaction isolation only gets you so far—it clicks much faster when you can run queries and watch the internals step by step.
That's why I built SQL in Depth, a free, open-source interactive textbook covering SQL and database internals from first principles. Everything runs right in the browser with no accounts, no paywalls, and no local DB setup.
Try it live: sql-in-depth.vedgupta.in


Source code on GitHub: github.com/innovatorved/sql-in-depth




  
  
  What's Inside




Interactive WASM SQLite 3 Workbench — write and run real SQLite 3 queries directly in the browser alongside each lesson.
Table-Level Relational Visualizer — watch how joins, filters, groupings, and transformations operate on actual rows step by step.
180 Structured Units — from relational algebra and core SQL semantics to indexing, query optimization, storage internals, and transactions.
36 Interactive Simulators — experiment hands-on with database internals and see how design trade-offs behave.
If you're preparing for backend interviews, sharpening your SQL fundamentals, or curious about how relational engines work under the hood, give it a spin!
If you find it useful, a star on GitHub helps others discover it—and issues, PRs, or ideas for new simulators are always welcome in the comments or on GitHub.
articles.title: SQL in Depth: Interactive WASM SQLite 3 Workbench & Database Internals from First Principles

Both are dedicated to the public domain under CC0 1.0. The same files are also on Hugging Face.

It's been almost a year now since I stepped into the world of agentic coding and Spec-Driven Development. Before, I really hated it, because the quality of LLM-s was poor. Writing specifications, refining them with the agents, validation against rules, system design and existing requirements - it became new routine in my projects.
Agentic coding did not increase my speed in many places, but instead shifted the effort from writing code to the discovery and design phase. And there are some new extra benefits of it: things that previously happened in my head, are now documented. There are written artifacts: specifications, decision logs, architecture documentations, that previously we…
